📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — find the bias, name its source

WORKED EXAMPLE — three biased systems, three sources
• A résumé screener trained on a decade of past hires downgrades women’s colleges → historical/training-data bias (the data encodes past discrimination).
• A face unlock that fails dark-skinned users → representation/sampling bias (underrepresented groups in training images).
• A crime-prediction tool sends more patrols where more crime was RECORDED, generating more records there → feedback-loop bias (the system amplifies its own outputs).
Mitigations by stage: diversify/rebalance data → fairness-aware training → outcome audits by group → human review + monitoring. Fairness itself has competing definitions (equal accuracy? equal approval rates?) — say WHICH you’re using.
⚠️ BIAS ENTERS THROUGH DATA MORE THAN CODE
“Where does AI bias usually come from?” → the training data (and the metric), not a programmer’s malicious if-statement. Detection = disaggregated evaluation (metrics per subgroup).
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

AI systems trained on biased data produce biased outputs. The phrase 'algorithmic bias' has appeared in headlines about hiring tools that disfavored women, lending models that disfavored minorities, healthcare algorithms that systematically underserved Black patients. Understanding bias — its sources, manifestations, and mitigations — is essential to building AI that doesn't quietly perpetuate harm.

Core concepts

1. Bias enters through every stage. Training data: reflects historical patterns including discriminatory ones. Labeling: annotators bring their own biases. Model design: optimization targets that proxy for what you want but aren't equivalent. Deployment: who the system is used on, in what context. No single point to audit; must consider the whole pipeline.

2. Historical bias. Past data reflects past discrimination. Hiring data from a male-dominated industry has fewer female applicants and successes; train a model on it and the model 'learns' to disfavor women. The model isn't malicious — it's accurate to the past, which is what's wrong.

3. Representation and sampling bias. Training data underrepresents some groups. Facial recognition systems trained mostly on light-skinned faces fail on darker-skinned faces. Voice recognition trained on standard accents fails on regional accents. Underrepresentation = worse performance for underrepresented groups.

4. Measurement bias. What you measure isn't what you mean. 'Healthcare cost' as a proxy for 'health need' undercounts groups historically denied care. 'Productive employee' measured by hours logged misses unmeasured contributions. The proxy/target gap is where bias hides.

5. Disparate impact, with or without intent. Even systems designed without discriminatory intent can produce disparate outcomes. US law treats some kinds of disparate impact as actionable in employment and credit. The standard isn't 'did you mean to discriminate' — it's 'do outcomes disproportionately disadvantage protected groups, and is there business justification?'

6. Mitigations. Audit training data for representation. Define and measure fairness metrics relevant to the task (equal opportunity, calibration, demographic parity — they're not all simultaneously achievable). Test model outcomes by group. Build in human review for consequential decisions. Document model behavior (model cards). Ongoing monitoring for drift.

7. The fundamental tension. Different fairness definitions are mathematically incompatible. You can have equal false-positive rates across groups, OR equal calibration, OR equal positive prediction rates — but not all three when base rates differ. Choosing among them is itself a values decision; pretending fairness is a single solvable property obscures the choice.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Removing protected attributes from training data and assuming bias is gone — proxies remain.
  • Choosing 'accurate' as a synonym for 'fair' — accurate predictions of biased outcomes propagate the bias.
  • Auditing once and considering it done — drift makes auditing continuous.
  • Pretending technical solutions fully address what are partly social and political problems.

Quick recap

Bias enters AI through historical data, representation, measurement, and deployment. Disparate impact is actionable with or without intent. Mitigations require auditing data, defining and measuring relevant fairness metrics, testing by group, and ongoing monitoring. Different fairness definitions are mathematically incompatible — the choice among them is a values decision that must be made deliberately.

Glossary

Algorithmic bias
Systematic skew in AI outputs reflecting biased training data, design, or deployment.
Historical bias
Past discrimination encoded in training data.
Representation bias
Underrepresentation of groups in training data leading to worse model performance for them.
Disparate impact
Outcomes disproportionately disadvantaging protected groups, regardless of intent.
Fairness metric
Mathematical definition of fair outcomes; multiple incompatible definitions exist.

Bias enters through label errors (wrong ground truth teaches wrong lessons) and skewed sampling. Confirmation bias: teams unconsciously build and test in ways that confirm expectations. Mitigation: diverse training data and diverse teams. Detection: evaluate performance across demographic groups — a single overall accuracy number can hide a failing subgroup.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — an AI ethics review, run like a checklist

WORKED EXAMPLE — reviewing a school’s dropout-prediction system
• Transparency/explainability: can staff see WHY a student was flagged? Black-box denials of consequential outcomes fail the bar.
• Accountability: who owns errors — vendor, district, counselor? A named human must.
• Privacy: minors’ data → minimization, consent (FERPA/COPPA overlap).
• Fairness: audited by demographic group?
• Human oversight: flags INFORM counselors, never auto-punish.
• Beneficence/non-maleficence: does deployment help the flagged students or just surveil them?
Verdict pattern: permissible WITH conditions — the conditioned answer is almost always the graded one over ban/allow absolutes.
⚠️ CONSEQUENTIAL DECISIONS RAISE THE BAR
Grades, loans, hiring, parole: higher stakes demand more explainability, audit, and human review. Stakes-proportional oversight is the framework the exam rewards.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Ethics in AI is broader than bias. Privacy, transparency, accountability, autonomy, employment effects, environmental costs, concentration of power — each is a real and contested concern. Engineers and product designers make choices that touch all of these. Naming the issues and frameworks gives you the vocabulary to engage them deliberately.

Core concepts

1. Privacy and surveillance. AI scales surveillance: face recognition, voice analytics, behavioral inference. Combined data — location plus purchases plus communications — enables profiling no individual surveiller could match. The legal and ethical frameworks lag the capability. Privacy by design (chapter 4 of D333) is the engineering response.

2. Transparency and explainability. Can users and regulators understand why an AI made a decision? Some regulations (EU AI Act) require explanation for consequential decisions. Black-box models complicate this. Approaches: model cards, feature importance, counterfactual explanations. Trade-off with capability is real but smaller than it once was.

3. Accountability when AI errs. When an AI system causes harm, who is responsible? Developer, deployer, user, vendor? Diffusion of responsibility is itself a problem; it lets harm happen without a clear actor. Frameworks like the EU AI Act assign roles; case law is still developing.

4. Autonomy and manipulation. AI can manipulate at scale: personalized ads, targeted misinformation, recommendation loops. The ethical question is when persuasion becomes manipulation and when influence undermines autonomy. The lines are debated; the technology has run ahead of the consensus.

5. Employment effects. Automation has always shifted what humans do; AI accelerates and broadens it. The ethical questions: who bears transition costs (workers, communities, employers, society)? How are gains distributed? Is the goal to replace humans, augment them, or something else? Engineering choices contribute even when they don't decide.

6. Environmental costs. Training large models consumes substantial electricity, often from fossil-fueled grids. Inference at scale adds more. Water cooling at data centers adds local impacts. The numbers vary by source; the trend is large and growing. Reporting and reduction efforts are emerging but uneven.

7. Concentration of power. Frontier AI capability is concentrated in a few companies and countries. The compute, data, and expertise required exclude most participants. Implications for competition, sovereignty, dependency, and democratic accountability are substantial. Open models, public infrastructure, and policy frameworks all attempt to counterweight, with mixed success.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating ethics as someone else's problem — engineers shape what's possible.
  • Reducing ethics to compliance — compliance is a floor, not the ceiling.
  • Engaging ethics only after deployment, when changes are expensive.
  • Assuming technical solutions can fully address what are partly political and social problems.

Quick recap

AI ethics extends beyond bias to privacy, transparency, accountability, autonomy, employment, environmental costs, and concentration of power. Each issue is real and contested. Engineering choices touch all of them. Engaging ethics deliberately — surfacing concerns, designing for transparency, considering second-order effects — is part of professional responsibility.

Glossary

Explainability
Ability to articulate why an AI made a specific decision.
Algorithmic accountability
Frameworks assigning responsibility for AI-caused harms.
Manipulation vs persuasion
Contested line between influence that respects user autonomy and influence that undermines it.
Carbon footprint of AI
Environmental impact of training and inference, particularly at large model scale.
Compute concentration
Frontier AI capability requiring resources accessible only to a few organizations.

Ethical stakes: AI can widen inequality when gains concentrate narrowly. High-stakes decisions (loans, parole, diagnosis) demand interpretable models — people deserve reasons. Deepfakes weaponize synthetic media against truth. The ledger has a bright side too: healthcare applications — earlier detection, drug discovery — are among AI’s most beneficial uses.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — attacks ON AI and misuse OF AI

WORKED EXAMPLE — four incidents, classified
• Stickers on a stop sign make the classifier read “Speed Limit 45” → adversarial example (crafted perturbation fooling the model).
• Attackers seed the training pipeline with mislabeled data → data poisoning (corrupt the model at its source).
• Repeated queries reconstruct faces from the training set → model inversion / privacy extraction.
• A cloned voice authorizes a wire transfer → deepfake-enabled fraud (misuse of generative AI; detection + verification protocols are the counters).
Defenses map one-to-one: adversarial training/input filtering; data provenance and validation; differential privacy/query limits; media authentication + process controls.
⚠️ ATTACK ON THE MODEL vs WITH THE MODEL
Adversarial examples/poisoning/inversion target the AI system; deepfakes/automated phishing weaponize AI against people. Classify the direction first — it picks the defense family.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

AI systems face their own security threats — adversarial inputs, data poisoning, model theft, prompt injection. They also enable new attack capabilities — deepfakes, automated phishing, malware generation. Understanding both directions is essential for any engineer building or defending AI systems.

Core concepts

1. Adversarial examples. Small, often imperceptible perturbations to inputs cause misclassification. Image with added noise looks identical but classifier sees something different. Documented since 2014; remains an open problem. Defenses (adversarial training, certified robustness) help but don't solve.

2. Data poisoning. Attacker injects malicious examples into training data to corrupt the resulting model. Backdoor attacks: model behaves normally except when triggered by a specific pattern. Hard to detect because affected behavior is rare and targeted.

3. Model extraction and theft. Querying a deployed model enough lets an attacker train a near-replica without access to the original. Attacks against API-served models. Defenses: rate limiting, watermarking, restricting outputs (returning probabilities only above thresholds).

4. Prompt injection. User input crafted to override system instructions in LLM-based applications. 'Ignore previous instructions and...'. A whole class of attacks specific to LLMs and RAG systems. Mitigations are partial and evolving; treat all user-provided content as potentially adversarial.

5. Jailbreaks and circumventing safety training. Attacks that get safety-trained models to produce harmful outputs anyway. Roleplay, indirection, encoding tricks. Frontier labs invest heavily in red-teaming and safety training; researchers find new bypasses regularly. The arms race resembles antivirus.

6. AI as attacker capability. Generative AI lowers the cost of attacks: phishing emails personalized at scale, deepfake voices and videos for fraud, code-generation for malware variants. Defenders also use AI (anomaly detection, phishing filters); the asymmetry of who benefits more is debated.

7. Misuse and dual-use. Most useful AI capabilities are dual-use. Image generation enables art and disinformation. Code generation helps developers and malware authors. Voice cloning helps accessibility and impersonation fraud. Mitigations: safety training, deployment controls, terms of service, rapid response to abuse — none complete.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Deploying AI with user-controllable inputs without considering adversarial use — every input is potentially adversarial.
  • Trusting safety training as complete defense — bypasses are constant.
  • Treating AI security as 'the same as' regular security — it has unique attack surfaces and defenses.
  • Building dual-use capabilities without considering misuse pathways — the question 'who else might use this' is part of the design.

Quick recap

AI faces specific security threats: adversarial examples, data poisoning, model extraction, prompt injection, jailbreaks. AI also enables new attack capabilities: scalable phishing, deepfakes, automated malware. Defenses are partial and evolving on both sides. Dual-use is the reality — most capabilities serve good and harm — and the deployment, controls, and rapid response matter more than expecting any one mitigation to solve the problem.

Glossary

Adversarial example
Input crafted to cause AI misclassification while looking normal to humans.
Data poisoning
Injecting malicious examples into training data to corrupt the resulting model.
Prompt injection
User input crafted to override system instructions in LLM-based applications.
Jailbreak
Attack causing safety-trained models to produce restricted outputs.
Dual-use
Capabilities that can be used for both beneficial and harmful purposes.

Constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs)

📊 FIGURE — the steps, in order
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A CSP is a problem defined by three things: variables, a domain of values each can take, and constraints saying which combinations are allowed. Solving it means assigning a value to every variable so that all constraints hold. Map coloring, Sudoku, scheduling, and N-queens are all CSPs.

THE THREE INGREDIENTS
Variables (e.g., regions on a map), Domains (e.g., {red, green, blue}), Constraints (e.g., adjacent regions differ). A solution is a complete, consistent assignment.
⚙️ WHAT'S REALLY HAPPENING

Backtracking search assigns variables one at a time; if a partial assignment violates a constraint, it backs up and tries a different value. Forward checking prunes: after assigning a variable, remove now-illegal values from neighbors' domains — if any domain empties, backtrack early. Arc consistency (AC-3) goes further, repeatedly enforcing that every value of one variable has a compatible value in each constrained neighbor.

WORKED EXAMPLE — map coloring

Color a map so no two adjacent regions share a color, with domain {R,G,B}.

ConceptHere
VariablesEach region
Domain{R, G, B}
ConstraintsAdjacent regions ≠ same color

Backtracking assigns colors region by region; forward checking removes a color from a neighbor the moment it's used.

📝 EXAM WORDING

A CSP = variables + domains + constraints; a solution is a complete, consistent assignment. Backtracking = depth-first assign/undo. Forward checking prunes neighbor domains after each assignment. Arc consistency (AC-3) enforces that every value has a compatible neighbor value. Heuristics: MRV (most-constrained variable) and least-constraining value.

🎯 OA-STYLE CHECK
In map coloring as a CSP, the constraints are:
  1. Regions must be red
  2. Adjacent regions must have different colors
  3. All regions same color
  4. Colors must be numeric
Show answer
B. The constraint is that no two adjacent regions share a color — a classic binary constraint over the color domain.

📖 Worked example — a hard search problem, computed

WORKED EXAMPLE — A* expansion order, step by step
Nodes with g (cost so far) + h (estimate): S→A g=1,h=4 (f=5); S→B g=2,h=2 (f=4); A→G g=1+5=6,h=0 (f=6); B→G g=2+3=5,h=0 (f=5).
Frontier after S: {A:5, B:4} → expand B (lowest f). Add B→G (f=5). Frontier {A:5, G:5} → tie; expand G? A? Either way G’s f=5 path (S→B→G, cost 5) beats the S→A→G cost 6 — A* returns S→B→G.
The discipline: maintain the frontier sorted by f = g + h, always expand the minimum, stop when the GOAL is expanded (not merely generated) — with an admissible h, that guarantees optimality. Show the frontier at each step and hard questions become bookkeeping.

Searching Like an Algorithm, Not a Human

Uninformed search differs only in how the frontier is ordered. BFS uses a FIFO queue, so it visits nodes in order of increasing depth; DFS uses a stack (or recursion), diving down one branch before backtracking. When neighbors are listed in a fixed order (e.g., alphabetical), the visit sequence is fully determined, so you can trace it deterministically.

Uniform-cost search (UCS) always expands the frontier node with the smallest path cost g. A* expands the node with the smallest f = g + h, combining the cost so far with an estimate h of the cost remaining. A* returns an optimal path whenever h is admissible — that is, h(n) never overestimates the true cost h*(n) to the goal. Between two admissible heuristics, the one with larger values everywhere dominates and expands fewer nodes.

Contrast this with greedy best-first search, which ignores g and orders the frontier by h alone. Greedy is fast but not optimal: a low heuristic can lure it down an expensive path.

For adversarial problems, minimax propagates values bottom-up: MAX nodes take the maximum of their children, MIN nodes the minimum. Alpha-beta pruning gives the same answer while skipping branches that cannot change the result — once a MIN node's value drops to or below the best value MAX already has (alpha), the rest of that MIN node's children are pruned. 📖 Worked example — a hard ML + ethics scenario

WORKED EXAMPLE — the 99% accurate model that’s useless
A fraud model scores 99% accuracy — but only 1% of transactions ARE fraud, so predicting “never fraud” also scores 99%. Diagnose with the confusion matrix: recall on the fraud class turns out to be 10% — it misses 90% of fraud.
Fixes: evaluate with precision/recall/F1 (not accuracy) on imbalanced data; rebalance training (oversample fraud); tune the decision threshold for the cost of misses vs false alarms.
Then the ethics layer: false positives freeze innocent customers’ cards — disparate impact must be audited by group, thresholds justified, and appeals available. Hard questions braid the math (metrics) with the ethics (who bears each error type) — answer both threads.

Turning Numbers Into Judgments

A binary classifier's results form a confusion matrix of true positives (TP), true negatives (TN), false positives (FP), and false negatives (FN). From these: accuracy = (TP+TN)/total, precision = TP/(TP+FP), recall = TP/(TP+FN), and F1 = 2·precision·recall/(precision+recall), which equals 2·TP/(2·TP+FP+FN). Accuracy can look excellent while precision or recall are poor, so always check the metric that matches the cost of each error type.

Decision trees split on the attribute that most reduces entropy, H = -Σ p·log2(p). A pure node has entropy 0; a 50/50 split has entropy 1 bit. Information gain is the parent's entropy minus the weighted entropy of the children.

k-NN classifies a query by majority vote of its k nearest training points using a distance metric — no training phase, just computation at query time.

A large gap between high training accuracy and low test accuracy signals overfitting (high variance); uniformly low accuracy signals underfitting (high bias). Gradient descent updates a parameter against the slope: θ ← θ − α·(∂J/∂θ). A perceptron computes net = Σ wᵢxᵢ + b and fires 1 if net ≥ 0, else 0.

Finally, high overall accuracy does not imply fairness. A model can be accurate on aggregate yet inflict disparate impact on a subgroup — a reason to measure error rates per group, not just overall. Compute each answer below.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.

📋 AI Foundations

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

What is AI

⚠ AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DEEP LEARNING All deep learning is ML; all ML is AI; but AI includes non-learning approaches (rules, search). Options equating AI with ML are the standard distractor.

History and Evolution of AI

⚠ THE WINTERS HAVE A MORAL What caused AI winters? → expectations exceeding capability, then funding cuts. The modern relevance question ( could it happen again? ) expects that same mechanism.

Types of AI: Narrow, General, Super

⚠ IMPRESSIVE ≠ GENERAL Fluency across many topics is not general intelligence — LLMs remain narrow AI. Marking an existing product as AGI is the designed wrong answer.

"},"D681/cheat/c2":{"body":"

📋 AI Approaches

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Symbolic and Rule-Based AI

⚠ FORWARD = FROM FACTS; BACKWARD = FROM GOAL Starts with data and derives conclusions → forward chaining. Starts with a hypothesis and seeks supporting facts → backward. The direction is the exam question.

Machine Learning Basics

⚠ OVERFITTING IN ONE SENTENCE A model that memorizes training data (perfect train accuracy, poor test accuracy) has overfit — the reason held-out evaluation exists. This vocabulary anchors half the ML questions.

Neural Networks and Deep Learning

⚠ WEIGHTS LEARN; ARCHITECTURE IS CHOSEN Training adjusts weights/biases via backprop — it does not add layers. And why deep learning now? Data + GPU compute + algorithmic advances — the same trio from the history section. When a question asks why deep learning took off after 2012, name all three.

"},"D681/cheat/c3":{"body":"

Knowledge Representation

Core concepts — 1. The representation question. How do you encode facts about the world? 'Birds fly' — propositional? logical? a probability? a graph? a vector? Each representation…

Quick recap — Representations choose what's easy to express and infer. Propositional logic is foundational but limited. First-order logic adds quantifiers and predicates. Semantic…

Search Algorithms

⚠ ADMISSIBLE = NEVER OVERESTIMATES A* s optimality guarantee lives or dies on the heuristic never exceeding true remaining cost. What makes A* optimal? → admissible (consistent) heuristic — the single most-tested fact.

Reasoning vs Knowledge

⚠ DEDUCTION vs INDUCTION vs ABDUCTION Certain-from-rules → deduction. Pattern-from-examples → induction (ML s engine). Best-explanation-from-effect → abduction. Three words, three exam questions.

📋 AI Applications

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Computer Vision

⚠ CLASSIFY vs DETECT vs SEGMENT Whole-image label → classification. Boxes → detection. Pixel-level masks → segmentation. The exam hands you a task description and wants the right level.

Natural Language Processing

⚠ EMBEDDINGS = MEANING AS GEOMETRY The exam s favorite NLP concept: words/documents as vectors, similarity as distance. Which representation captures semantic similarity? → embeddings, not bag-of-words.

Recommendation Systems

⚠ COLD START BELONGS TO COLLABORATIVE New item has no ratings — which approach struggles? → collaborative filtering. Content-based handles new items (they have features) but struggles with new USERS unknown tastes.

Robotics and Decision Systems

⚠ THE LOOP IS THE ANSWER SHAPE How does a robot/agent operate? → sense → plan/decide → act, repeated. Naming which stage a described failure lives in (bad sensing? bad planning?) is the applied question.

📋 AI Ethics, Bias, and Security

Condensed from your lessons — the rules, traps and topics of this chapter in one place.

Bias in AI

⚠ BIAS ENTERS THROUGH DATA MORE THAN CODE Where does AI bias usually come from? → the training data (and the metric), not a programmer s malicious if-statement. Detection = disaggregated evaluation (metrics per…

Ethical Issues in AI

⚠ CONSEQUENTIAL DECISIONS RAISE THE BAR Grades, loans, hiring, parole: higher stakes demand more explainability, audit, and human review. Stakes-proportional oversight is the framework the exam rewards.

AI Security and Misuse

⚠ ATTACK ON THE MODEL vs WITH THE MODEL Adversarial examples/poisoning/inversion target the AI system; deepfakes/automated phishing weaponize AI against people. Classify the direction first — it picks the defense: robust training and data validation protect the model; detection tools and policy protect people from misuse.
